note: Breaks the LLM as judge pattern that many evaluation and RLAIF pipelines depend on.
title: Optimization-based Prompt Injection Attack to LLM-as-a-Judge
journal: Proceedings of the ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security

reading.body:
This paper breaks the LLM-as-judge pattern, where one model is used to evaluate another model's output, which many evaluation and reinforcement-learning pipelines currently depend on.

If the judge model itself can be manipulated through prompt injection, then any pipeline that trusts its verdict, whether for benchmarking or for training signal, inherits that vulnerability. This matters beyond security research because LLM-as-judge has become a common, cheap substitute for human evaluation across the industry, and this paper shows that substitute has a specific, demonstrated weakness.

The paper does not evaluate how widely LLM-as-judge is actually deployed in production training pipelines, only that the pattern itself can be attacked.

explain_beginner: Companies increasingly use AI systems to judge which answers are best. This paper shows that attackers can sneak hidden instructions into their responses to trick the judging AI into picking their answer every time, regardless of quality. Researchers created an automated attack method that finds exactly what to hide in a response to manipulate the judge. They tested defenses but found them ineffective, revealing a serious vulnerability in how AI evaluation systems work today.
explain_business: Organizations using AI judges to evaluate responses face a critical vulnerability. Attackers can manipulate the judging process to force selection of their content by embedding invisible instructions in responses. This undermines systems that automate quality assessment, recommendation ranking, and AI model training through feedback. Current protective measures fail to stop sophisticated attacks. Organizations should pause reliance on LLM judges for high-stakes decisions until stronger safeguards are developed, or implement additional human review layers for critical evaluation tasks.
explain_practitioner: This work presents JudgeDeceiver, an optimization-based prompt injection attack targeting LLM-as-a-Judge systems. The authors formulate the attack as an optimization problem and employ gradient-based methods to discover adversarial sequences that, when embedded in candidate responses, consistently cause the judge model to select them across diverse queries. Evaluation demonstrates superior effectiveness compared to manual prompt injection and jailbreak baselines. The attack succeeds in three application domains: LLM-based search, reinforcement learning from AI feedback, and tool selection. Tested defenses including perplexity-based filtering prove insufficient against the attack.
